summary: A companion to the BGP-4 specification that describes how BGP is applied in the Internet. It was a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 1772.

eli5.summary: A guide on how to actually use BGP. A newer version replaced it.

questions: how to use bgp in the internet
how to deploy bgp in the internet
subtitle: How BGP-4 routing protocol is deployed and configured in the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet needs a way for large networks (autonomous systems) to exchange routing information and enforce their own policies about which routes to use, especially as the Internet grows and faces address space exhaustion.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-4 is an exterior gateway protocol where border routers in each autonomous system exchange full AS paths with each other, allowing each AS to make routing decisions based on policy, performance, and path length.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as a companion to the BGP-4 protocol specification (RFC 1654), explaining practical deployment, topology models, policy configuration, and interaction with other protocols. It was replaced by RFC 1772.

today: RFC 1655 is a historic document that was obsoleted by RFC 1772 in 1994. It served as the practical companion to the BGP-4 protocol specification, but its guidance on deployment and policy has been superseded.

sections.title: Why BGP and the Internet's Scaling Challenges
sections.content:
The Internet was facing serious scaling problems in 1994. Class-B network addresses were being exhausted because they were too large for many organizations but the smaller Class-C addresses were too small. Routing tables in core routers were growing unmanageably. BGP-4, combined with Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), was designed to slow this growth by allowing routers to aggregate routing information and reduce the number of routes they had to maintain.

This RFC describes how BGP-4 is used in the Internet in practice, as a companion to the protocol specification. The Internet is modeled as a collection of arbitrarily connected Autonomous Systems (AS), each under single administrative control, using BGP to communicate between AS boundaries and interior routing protocols within each AS.
sections.eli5: The Internet was getting too big, with too many routes to remember. BGP-4 lets big networks tell each other about the routes they know without keeping a separate list for every tiny piece of the Internet.

sections.title: AS Topology Models and BGP Relationships
sections.content:
The RFC defines three types of autonomous systems based on their role in carrying traffic. A stub AS connects to only one other AS and carries only its own traffic. A multihomed AS connects to multiple AS's but refuses to carry transit traffic for others. A transit AS connects to multiple AS's and is designed to carry both local and transit traffic under policy restrictions.

BGP speakers (routers running BGP) within the same AS communicate via Internal BGP, while speakers in different AS's communicate via External BGP. A key requirement is that all BGP speakers representing the same AS must present a consistent image to the outside world, enforced by having consistent routing policies and information among them.
sections.eli5: Some networks are just customers with one connection. Others have multiple paths but don't let other people's traffic cross them. The biggest networks let traffic cross, but only according to their rules. BGP keeps track of which kind each network is.

sections.title: Route Aggregation and Information Control
sections.content:
BGP-4 requires implementations to support route aggregation, where a border router can announce a single aggregate prefix representing many subnets even if not all of them are currently reachable. This is the key mechanism for controlling routing table growth. BGP speakers must be able to specify when aggregated routes may be generated, handle deaggregation (announcing more specific routes), and handle overlapping routes by choosing to install the less specific route, more specific route, both, or neither.

By default, a BGP speaker should aggregate subnet routes to their corresponding network-level routes. However, fine-grained control of aggregation is required to support different routing policies that may depend on route origin or other characteristics.
sections.eli5: Instead of telling everyone about every tiny piece of your network, you can announce one big block that covers them all. This keeps route tables smaller.

sections.title: Policy Making and Path Selection
sections.content:
A multihomed AS can use BGP policy to refuse to carry traffic destined to other AS's, becoming a purely local network. It can also become a selective transit AS for only a subset of its neighbors. An AS can use various criteria to select preferred paths: shorter AS paths, quality metrics learned outside BGP (like bandwidth or latency), path origin (routes learned purely from BGP are preferred over those learned via EGP or other means), and presence or absence of specific AS's in the path. Fundamental to BGP is the rule that an AS advertises only the routes it actually uses, following the hop-by-hop routing paradigm.

Path selection is formally defined by mapping each full AS path to a degree of preference value; the path with the highest preference is selected. The RFC recommends that implementations support at least these policies: controlling which routes are announced to adjacent AS's, assigning explicit preference values to paths from particular neighbors, and suppressing routes that pass through particular AS's.
sections.eli5: Network operators can tell BGP: 'Use this path because I trust this backbone,' or 'Never route traffic through that network,' or 'Shorter paths are better.' Each network makes its own rules.

sections.title: Coexistence with Older Protocols
sections.content: Many networks in 1994 still used older exterior routing protocols like EGP2 and BGP-3. The RFC provides guidelines for graceful migration and coexistence. A BGP speaker can participate in both BGP-4 and BGP-3 or EGP2 simultaneously. When injecting BGP-4 information into EGP2, care must be taken to avoid information explosion if a single BGP prefix represents a set of consecutive legacy Class-A, B, or C networks; implementations must support options for controlled deaggregation. Similarly, when a BGP-4 speaker injects routes into BGP-3, it must convert BGP-4's AS_SET path attributes into AS_SEQUENCE format. Exchange of routing information between different protocols can only occur at domain boundaries.
sections.eli5: Old networks still used older routing protocols. BGP-4 speakers can talk to old-style networks, but they have to be careful about how they translate the information so it doesn't explode into too many routes.

sections.title: Operations over Switched Virtual Circuits
sections.content: For wide-area networks that use switched virtual circuit (SVC) services instead of permanent links, BGP can operate without continuously sending KEEPALIVE messages, which saves cost. This mode is selected by setting the Hold Time to zero in the BGP OPEN message. The circuit manager must detect link layer failures and notify TCP, which flushes the transmit queue and aborts the connection. On recovery, the circuit manager notifies TCP to resume. Some implementations use a periodic two-way poll between the BGP process and the circuit manager to detect if either has crashed, ensuring both stay coordinated.
sections.eli5: For networks that charge per minute of connection time, BGP can stop saying 'hello' periodically, saving money, as long as something else on the network is watching for problems.
